FACTS OF THE CASE 1.
Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that on 16.03.2021, at about 11:30 a.m., one Ms. Asha (since deceased) along with her brother namely Deepak had gone to Patparganj in search of a job.

It has been alleged that when they were going towards Azad apartment, in front of gate no. 2 of the Max hospital, Patparganj, Delhi, near metro pillar no. 211, within the jurisdiction of PS Madhu Vihar, a motorcycle (make Bullet) hit the above said Ms. Asha, due to which she fell down on the road and came under the wheels of one incoming truck bearing registration no. DL-1GC-2946 (hereinafter referred to as offending vehicle).

It has been further alleged that the said offending vehicle (truck)
was being driven by its driver i.e. respondent no. 1 (R1) herein, in a rash and negligent manner without taking necessary precautions at the time of the accident.
The victim was thereon rushed to Max hospital, where she died during the course of treatment on 23.03.2021.
The postmortem on the body of the deceased was thereon conducted at mortuary of Lal Bahadur Shastri Hospital, vide PM Report no. 147/21.

An FIR in this regard also came to be registered at PS Madhu Vihar, vide FIR no.
58/21, for the offences u/s 279/337/304-A IPC.
The present DAR petition thereafter came to be filed in due course for the petitioners being the LRs of the deceased/victim and against the respondents on 18.05.2022.

Issue wise findings Issue no.1 Whether respondent no.1 was driving the offending vehicle no.
DL-1GC-2946 on 16.03.2021 at about 11:30 am near Max hospital, PPG Delhi within the jurisdiction of PS Madhu Vihar in a rash and negligent manner and caused the death of deceased Ms. Asha?

OPP HARUN PRATAP PRATAP Date:
2026.01.03 17:52:05 +0530 11.
In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is tested on the touchstone of principle of preponderance of probabilities.

It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.

The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.

Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi & Ors. Vs Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs Amir Chand & Ors, 2011 (1) SCR 1906 (Civil Appeal No. 1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co. ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.

sentences.text: In the present case, the petitioners have examined the brother of the deceased namely Deepak who also happened to be an eye witness of the accident as their star witness to prove the contentions regarding the claim for compensation, apart from examining the mother of the deceased as PW-1 and PW-2 respectively.
Both the said witnesses have categorically stated in their examination on oath that the accident was caused due to rash and negligent act of respondent no. 1 being driver of the offending vehicle.

HARUN PRATAP Date:
PRATAP 2026.01.03 17:52:09 +0530 The said contentions are duly corroborated by the findings of the police as mentioned in the FIR, charge-sheet, site plan,
postmortem report along with other documents pertaining to criminal case in respect of the incident in question brought on record as Ex. PW1/6 (colly) and no ground has been made out by the respondents to disbelieve the same.

The PW-1 has specifically deposed about the mode and manner of the accident and has even stated about the registration number of offending vehicle clearly, while deposing that the offending vehicle came from the backside in a rash and negligent manner.

The PW-1 has even stated during his cross-examination that the driver of the offending vehicle i.e. R-1,
ought to have been careful when he along with his sister had fallen down on the road after being hit by a bullet motorcycle.

The PW-1 has further specifically denied the suggestion that the accident occured due to rash and negligent driving of the motorcycle driver and not by the rash and negligent driving of R-1.
13.

The sole defence taken by the respondents in this case is that the victim had been initially hit by the bullet motorcycle rider and that the rashness and negligence was on the part of the motorcycle rider only.

However, it is pertinent to note that the accident in this case took place in front of a hospital and perusal of the CCTV footage of the incident in question makes it evident that the offending vehicle was being indeed driven in a rash and negligent manner by R-1 without taking necessary precautions.

The spot of the accident being a busy public place is invariably being used by the pedestrians and as such, the driver of the offending vehicle is expected to be extra vigilant and careful while driving his vehicle at such place, but the reasonable standard of care and caution has not been exercised by the R-1 in driving the offending vehicle at the time of accident.

Though, it is an admitted fact that the victim and the PW-1 were hit by a HARUN by HARUN PRATAP PRATAP Date: 2026.01.03 17:52:14 +0530 bullet motorcycle firstly, but the petitioners have opted to seek compensation against the driver and owner of the offending vehicle only.

Hence, the Tribunal refrains from passing any observation regarding the quantum of negligence on part of the motorcycle rider as the latter has not been impleaded as a respondent by the petitioners to seek compensation.

Even otherwise, the composite negligence on part of the motorcycle rider does not absolve the liability on part of the driver of the offending vehicle while the latter has been specifically found to be rash and negligent in his driving of the offending vehicle, by the police in its charge-sheet filed before the concerned Court.

At the same time, no material has been brought on record by the respondents to disbelieve the testimony of PW-1, while the fact that the offending vehicle hit the deceased victim after suddenly coming from backside is ipso-facto sufficient proof of rash and negligent act on part of the driver of the offending vehicle.

The position of law has been recently reiterated by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as "Ranjeet & Anr. Vs. Abdul Kayam Neb & Anr." Arising out of SLP (C ) No.
10351/2019, wherein it has been held that:-
"It is settled in law that once a charge-sheet has been filed and the driver has been held negligent, no further evidence is required to prove that the bus was being negligently driven by the bus driver.

17. In view of the above, it could be safely assumed that the offending vehicle was being driven by R-1 indeed at the time of incident and the fatal injuries to the deceased took place on account of the incident in question itself.

18. Having ruled so, this Tribunal now proceeds to assess the wrongful act, neglect or default of R-1,
if any, in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
Admittedly, R-1 has not explained the circumstances under which his vehicle (i.e. the offending vehicle) hit the deceased Ms. Asha.

In the absence of any averment or evidence regarding any mechanical defect in the offending vehicle or any material depicting any negligent/sudden act or omission on the part of the deceased or any other such person, the only inference possible in the given facts and circumstances is that of neglect and default on the part of R-1 in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.

In view of the above discussion, this tribunal is constrained to hold R-1 guilty of gross neglect and default in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time leading to the fatal injuries to the deceased Ms.
Asha.

Therefore, in view of the above discussion, this Tribunal holds that the deceased Ms. Asha suffered fatal injuries on account of neglect and default of R-1 while driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
The issue at hand is thus decided against the respondents and in favour of the petitioners.

LIABILITY 23.
Now, the question arises as to which of the respondents is liable to pay the compensation amount.
Herein, it is pertinent to note that the offending vehicle was not insured at the time of alleged accident.
As held above, the respondent no. 1 being driver of the offending vehicle at the time of the incident is the principal tort feasor in the present case.
As far as HARUN PRATAP PRATAP 2026.01.03 17:52:33 +0530 vicarious liability of the owner of the offending vehicle is concerned
, it is pertinent to note that the registered owner of the offending vehicle in the present case happened to be EDMC/MCD.
It is an admitted fact on record that the offending vehicle remained registered in the name of the said owner even on the date of the accident in question.

24. Therefore, in view of the afore-said facts and circumstances, the Tribunal has no hesitation in hereby arriving at the finding that the liability to make the payment of compensation amount in this case is of R1 and R2 jointly and severally.
The issue at hand is accordingly decided in favour of the petitioners and against the respondents.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is tested on the touchstone of principle of preponderance of probabilities.
It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.
The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.
Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi & Ors. Vs Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs Amir Chand & Ors, 2011 (1) SCR 1906 (Civil Appeal No. 1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co. ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.

Both the said witnesses have categorically stated in their examination on oath that the accident was caused due to rash and negligent act of respondent no. 1 being driver of the offending vehicle.
The sole defence taken by the respondents in this case is that the victim had been initially hit by the bullet motorcycle rider and that the rashness and negligence was on the part of the motorcycle rider only.
The spot of the accident being a busy public place is invariably being used by the pedestrians and as such, the driver of the offending vehicle is expected to be extra vigilant and careful while driving his vehicle at such place, but the reasonable standard of care and caution has not been exercised by the R-1 in driving the offending vehicle at the time of accident.
Even otherwise, the composite negligence on part of the motorcycle rider does not absolve the liability on part of the driver of the offending vehicle while the latter has been specifically found to be rash and negligent in his driving of the offending vehicle, by the police in its charge-sheet filed before the concerned Court.
At the same time, no material has been brought on record by the respondents to disbelieve the testimony of PW-1, while the fact that the offending vehicle hit the deceased victim after suddenly coming from backside is ipso-facto sufficient proof of rash and negligent act on part of the driver of the offending vehicle.
Furthermore, respondent no. 1 i.e. driver of the offending vehicle and respondent no. 2 i.e. owner of the offending vehicle have neither impeached HARUN PRATAP PRATAP 2026.01.03 17:52:23 +0530 the testimony of PW-1 & PW-2 nor they have led any defence evidence to substantiate their claim that the accident was caused due to fault of the deceased or that they have been falsely implicated in the present case.
Admittedly, R-1 has not explained the circumstances under which his vehicle (i.e. the offending vehicle) hit the deceased Ms. Asha.
In the absence of any averment or evidence regarding any mechanical defect in the offending vehicle or any material depicting any negligent/sudden act or omission on the part of the deceased or any other such person, the only inference possible in the given facts and circumstances is that of neglect and default on the part of R-1 in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
In view of the above discussion, this tribunal is constrained to hold R-1 guilty of gross neglect and default in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time leading to the fatal injuries to the deceased Ms.
Asha.
Hence, the petitioners being LRs i.e. mother and father of the deceased are entitled to compensation in this case as the claim of the petitioners being dependent of the deceased has neither been denied nor disputed in any manner by the respondents during the entire proceedings.
It is an admitted fact on record that the offending vehicle remained registered in the name of the said owner even on the date of the accident in question.
It is clear from above stated facts and circumstances that the deceased had expired soon after the accident and no medical expenditure was undertaken by the petitioners in the treatment of the deceased before her death.
Hence, petitioners are not entitled to any compensation under this head on account of absence of any evidence brought on record in this regard.
In the present case, perusal of the Aadhar card and registration certificate of matriculation of deceased Ms. Asha Ex. PW1/2 (colly) reveals that date of birth of the deceased was 07.07.1994 and the same has not been disputed in any manner by the respondents.
However, the petitioners have duly brought on record the 10 th class certificate of the deceased showing that she was matriculate at the time of the accident and the said fact has neither been denied nor been disputed in any manner by the respondents.
Therefore, this Tribunal has assessed the income of deceased at parity with minimum wages of a "Clerical-Matriculates" in the State of Delhi, prevalent at the time of accident i.e. Rs. 18,797/- per month on the date of accident.

(2017) 16 SCC 680", 40% addition shall be given to the deceased towards future prospects as she was below 40 years at the time of incident and she was self employed.
Therefore, both the two petitioners shall be treated as dependent of the deceased for the purpose of the present petition.
Therefore, in the entire given facts and circumstances, deduction of half of total income is made for personal living expenses of deceased.
Hence, an amount of Rs. 13,158/- (Rs. 26,316/2) is required to be deducted from monthly income of deceased.
